story.about: Chapters for the Story tab of the Uses & studies drawer (site/js/stories.js). Rules: numbers with source.kind='study' are printed in the cited PDF in bibliography/ (page recorded); source.kind='app' numbers are this app's analysis of its own served data (method named, details in DATA_REPORT.md); no causal claims beyond the cited papers; at most two key numbers per chapter and none that the text already states; per-chapter citations live in 'sources' (collapsed in the UI). status='pending' chapters show their placeholder until the named work lands. visual.highlight draws the Nyando river highlight; story labels (Mau, Nyando, Kano plains, Winam Gulf, Kisumu) show whenever the story is open.
story.title: From the Mau to the lake
story.note: Study numbers are as printed in the cited papers (pages in story_chapters.json); “this app's analysis” numbers come from the app's own data (methods in the data report).

chapters.title: From the Mau to the lake
chapters.text: Lake Victoria's basin gathers rain from highlands in five East African countries - the Mau escarpment among them - and drains it through rivers like the Nyando into the world's second-largest freshwater lake. This story follows that water: the rains, the lake's record levels, the floods, the droughts, and the land the water crosses. Scroll on; the map follows each chapter.
sources: Five countries (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi): Mugo et al. (2020), Remote Sensing 12, 2829 · p.1

chapters.title: The short rains of 2019
chapters.text: Late 2019 brought exceptional rain. On the map, the October-December 2019 rainfall anomaly stands out across the basin; the chart tracks each year's short rains. Khaki & Awange (2021) found the September-November short rains had the dominant effect on the lake's rise that followed, with a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole identified as the main cause of the above-average rains. This app's short-rains season is October–December; Khaki & Awange used September–November.

numbers.label: OND 2019 basin rainfall, vs a 381 mm OND normal (1991-2020)

source.method: CHIRPS v3.0 basin mean, land cells only

sources: SON 2019 rains dominant; IOD the main driver: Khaki & Awange (2021), Sensors 21, 4304 · abstract p.1; sect. 4.5 p.14

chapters.title: A lake at record levels
chapters.text: The lake answered within months. Pietroiusti et al. (2024) measure a 1.21 m rise in the six months to 17 May 2020, to a record 13.46 m on the Jinja gauge - a 63-year event in the current climate. The satellite altimetry series in the chart shows the same climb, and a new record in May 2024.

visual.note: The Jinja gauge (13.46 m) and the satellite series (~1,135 m) use different datums: a local gauge zero versus elevation above sea level.

charts.title: Lake level, monthly mean (m, DAHITI altimetry)

source.method: DAHITI (DGFI-TUM) series served by this app

sources: 1.21 m; 13.46 m on the Jinja gauge; 63-year event: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), ESD 15, 225-264 · abstract p.225; sect. 1.1 p.227 (gauge: sect. 2 p.229); sect. 3.5 p.237

chapters.title: Where the water went
chapters.text: Around the rising lake, water spread over the floodplains. The map shows the water that Sentinel-1 radar observed at least once between April and July 2020, outside the lake's 2011-2015 extent. In the Nzoia-Yala floodplain and on the Speke Gulf shore it agrees with Pietroiusti et al. (2024). Their additional flooding east of the Speke Gulf head is not confirmed by GFM's algorithms or by JRC Global Surface Water.

visual.note: ≤ 312.3 km² of water outside the 2011–2015 lake within 50 km of the shore (upper bound: measured over 1 Apr–31 Jul 2020, which contains Pietroiusti et al.'s 5 Apr–1 Jul window), against their ~642.5 km². Ours is the GFM ensemble water extent minus a static lake mask; theirs is HASARD flood detections. April 2020 could not be checked optically because of cloud, and part of the area east of the Speke Gulf head is outside GFM's mappable zone.

Ours is the GFM ensemble water extent minus a static lake mask; theirs is HASARD flood detections.

chapters.title: People in the water's way
chapters.text: Floods matter because people live on the plains the water takes. Pietroiusti et al. (2024) estimate that more than 29,000 people living within 50 km of the shoreline were affected by flooding over 5 Apr–1 Jul 2020. The map shows the years-flooded record over the Kano plains, where the Nyando meets the gulf.

exposure.label: people living in cells where water was detected in ≥ N years (2016–2025), WorldPop 2020
exposure.note: Not comparable to Pietroiusti et al.'s >29,000 for 2020: different metric (people in cells ever flooded vs people affected in one event) and period.

sources: >29,000 people affected within 50 km, 5 Apr–1 Jul 2020: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), ESD 15, 225-264 · window: methods sect. 2.1.1 p.228; number: sect. 3.2 p.232 (the abstract, p.225, says "between April and July")
People in cells flooded in ≥ N years: this app's analysis, GFM years flooded 2016–2025 × WorldPop 2020 (DATA_REPORT §2, Population)

chapters.title: When the rains run short
chapters.text: The same rains that flood can fail. The figure sets the drenched end of 2019 beside August 2026, when the basin's three-month rainfall was moderately dry (basin-mean SPI-3 −1.13, June–August; provisional). The chart tracks the basin-mean SPI-3 through both floods and the dry spells between them. Liu et al. (2022) modelled the basin's runoff droughts as generally aggravated under the 1985-to-2014 land-cover change, particularly in the central-western and eastern basin.

visual.alt: SPI-3 maps: December 2019 wet versus August 2026 dry
visual.note: Liu et al. modelled runoff drought (3-month SRI); the app's SPI-3 is rainfall deficit - the two need not match.

source.method: SPI-3 from CHIRPS v3.0, gamma fit 1991-2020, basin land mean

sources: Drought aggravated (frequency, duration), central-western and eastern basin: Liu et al. (2022), Ecological Indicators 145, 109580 · abstract p.1; results pp.6, 8; conclusions p.9

chapters.title: The land the water crosses
chapters.text: Upstream, the basin's land has been changing. The map shows cumulative tree-cover loss over the Mau and the upper Nyando; the chart counts the basin's loss year by year. Mugo et al. (2020) record the basin's conversion to farmland and settlements between 1985 and 2014: small-scale farmland grew by over 90 %, urban areas by over 800 %.

visual.note: Sub-basins: HydroBASINS units for the Nzoia, Yala, Nyando and Sondu-Miriu (see the data report).

numbers.label: tree-cover loss in the basin, 2001-2025 (peak year 2017, 383 km²)

source.method: Hansen GFC-2025-v1.13, cover 2000 >= 30 %; loss, not deforestation

sources: Farmland +90 %, urban +800 %, 1985-2014: Mugo et al. (2020), Remote Sensing 12, 2829 · results p.9; table 2 p.10

chapters.title: What the rivers carry
chapters.text: Changed land sends more than water downstream. In the Nyando basin, geochemical fingerprinting of riverbed sediment points to the highland sub-catchments: the Nyando-Kipchorian and Ainamutua together account for most of the sampled sediment mixture, areas the authors describe as affected by cropping on steep slopes and deforestation.

visual.alt: Sediment source shares of the Nyando riverbed mixture
visual.note: Sub-catchments approximate, derived from HydroSHEDS using the outlet sample sites of Humphrey et al. (2025).

sources: Nyando-Kipchorian 44 ± 4 %, Ainamutua 39 ± 4 %, Awach Kano & Nyaidho 17 ± 7 %: Humphrey et al. (2025), Catena 255, 109053 · abstract p.1; sect. 3.2 p.5, fig. 5a

chapters.title: What we cannot see yet
chapters.text: Honest maps say where they end. Radar cannot assess floods everywhere - dense vegetation and towns hide them. Water quality is measurable from space in principle, but Warren et al. (2021) used no in-situ data for any of their 24 lakes, Lake Victoria included - field checks would come first.

numbers.label: tuned satellite-to-satellite - no field validation in any of them

sources: No in-situ validation for any study lake: Warren et al. (2021), RSE 265, 112651 · abstract p.1; introduction p.2

chapters.title: Explore it yourself
chapters.text: Every layer in this story is in the explorer: years flooded and flood frequency by season, rainfall and drought by month, population, land cover and tree-cover loss, and the lake's full altimetry record. The Studies tab holds the papers behind the numbers.

studies.about: Registry for the 'Uses & studies' drawer (site/js/stories.js). Rules: every number or claim in a kind='published' card was verified against the cited PDF in bibliography/ on 2026-10-23; 'verified' records where. Only figures stated in the paper - no percentages or values derived from its tables. kind='explore' cards carry a question only - no numbers, no claims.
studies.note: Published findings quote the cited paper (page and figure recorded in studies.json); explore cards are open questions, not claims.

cards.question: How unusual was the 2020 lake-level rise?
cards.finding: Lake Victoria rose by 1.21 m in the six months to 17 May 2020, reaching a record 13.46 m on the Jinja gauge - a 63-year event in the current climate, estimated 1.8 times as likely (95% CI 0.8-15.8) than in a pre-industrial climate.
cards.citation: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), Earth System Dynamics 15, 225-264

verified.claim: 1.21 m rise, Nov 2019 - 17 May 2020 (84% of the 1.44 m Sep 2019 - May 2020 rise); 'record-breaking level of 13.46 m measured in situ on 17 May 2020' - the in-situ record is the Jinja gauge (gauge datum, not metres a.s.l., hence 'on the Jinja gauge' in the finding)
verified.where: abstract p.225; sect. 1.1 p.227; in-situ series at Jinja: sect. 2 p.229; sect. 3.3 p.234

cards.caveat: The confidence interval includes 1, so the attribution to climate change is suggestive, not conclusive - the paper says so itself.

cards.question: What drove the 2019-2020 rise?
cards.finding: Satellite gravimetry and altimetry put the rise at ~1.4 m. Rainfall in the September-November 2019 short rains had the dominant effect, and a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole is identified as the main cause of the above-average rains.

verified.claim: ~1.4 m rise (1.387 m, mid-2020 vs the same time in 2019)
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 4 p.8; conclusions p.16

verified.claim: SON 2019 short rains dominant (MAM 2019 was also above average)
IOD the main driver (precipitation correlation 0.69; ENSO 0.32, NAO 0.27)
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 4.5 p.14; sect. 5 p.15

cards.caveat: This app's short-rains season is October–December; Khaki & Awange used September–November.

cards.question: Who was affected by the 2020 floods?
cards.finding: More than 29,000 people living within 50 km of the shoreline are estimated to have been affected by flooding over 5 Apr–1 Jul 2020, the paper's radar window, over a flooded area of about 642.5 km².
cards.citation: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), Earth System Dynamics 15, 225-264

verified.claim: 'more than 29 000 people... affected by floods between April and July 2020' (exact estimate 29,070, stated for Apr-Jun in table 1); 'affected', not displaced
verified.where: abstract p.225; sect. 3.2 p.232; table 1 p.235

verified.claim: flooded area ~642.5 km² within 50 km of the shores; SAR window 5 April 2020-1 July 2020
verified.where: window: methods sect. 2.1.1 p.228; area: sect. 3.2 p.232, fig. 5 p.237

cards.caveat: Our GFM flood layer agrees only partly with the paper's flood map - see DATA_REPORT §3.1 for where and why. The paper's text also calls this window April–July (sect. 3.2) and April–June (Fig. 5).

cards.question: Where did drought risk change as forest became farmland?
cards.finding: SWAT modelling of the basin under its 1985 versus 2014 land cover shows hydrological drought became more frequent and longer-lasting, particularly in the central-western and eastern basin where forest was massively converted to agricultural land. Agriculture grew from about 35 % to 65 % of the basin over that period; grassland shrank from 30 % to 10 %.

verified.claim: 'hydrological drought was generally aggravated with increased drought frequency and lengthened duration, particularly for the central western and eastern regions with massive conversion of forest to agricultural land'
verified.where: abstract p.1; results p.6 and p.8; conclusions p.9

verified.claim: method: SWAT run with the 1985 and 2014 LULC maps; droughts from the 3-month standardized runoff index (SRI <= -1)
'the agricultural area increased from approximately 35 % in 1985 to 65 % in 2014'; 'the grassland area decreased from 30 % in 1985 to 10 % in 2014'

cards.caveat: The app's SPI-3 shows rainfall deficit; the paper's droughts are runoff droughts (3-month SRI from a model), so the two patterns need not match.

cards.question: How has land use changed across the basin?
cards.finding: Between 1985 and 2014 forests, woodlands, grasslands and wetlands were converted to farmland and settlements: small-scale farmland grew by over 90%, from about 5.7 to 11.0 million hectares, urban areas grew by over 800%, and open grasslands declined by 41%.

verified.claim: conversion of forests, woodlands, grasslands, wetlands to farmlands or settlements, 1985-2014
small-scale farmlands +'over 90%', 5,656,113.81 ha (1985) to 11,016,723.51 ha (2014); urban +'over 800%'; open grasslands -41%; all as printed (no derived shares)

cards.caveat: Indicative change only: the app's land-cover layer (Esri/IO LULC, 2017-) is a different product and period than the paper's Landsat classification (1985-2014).

cards.question: Which sub-catchments supply the Nyando's sediment?
cards.finding: Geochemical fingerprinting of riverbed sediment apportions the Nyando catchment's sediment mixture to the Nyando-Kipchorian (44 ± 4 %) and Ainamutua (39 ± 4 %) sub-catchments - highland areas affected by cropping on steep slopes and deforestation - with 17 ± 7 % from the Awach Kano and Nyaidho.

verified.claim: Nyando-Kipchorian 44 ± 4 %, Ainamutua 39 ± 4 %, Awach Kano and Nyaidho 17 ± 7 % of the Nyando riverbed-sediment end-point mixture
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 3.2 p.5, fig. 5a; conclusions p.12

cards.caveat: These are modelled shares of the riverbed sediment sampled within the Nyando basin, not measured sediment flux to Lake Victoria. Rivers are drawn on the map; the Nyando's headwaters are the highlands in view.

cards.question: Could the app show water quality in the lake?
cards.finding: Chlorophyll-a and turbidity algorithms for Sentinel-2 can be aligned with Sentinel-3 so the two sensors give complementary observations, and Lake Victoria is among the 24 lakes tuned. But the study is satellite-to-satellite: no in-situ measurements were used for any lake, Lake Victoria included.
cards.citation: Warren et al. (2021), Remote Sensing of Environment 265, 112651

verified.claim: MSI tuned against OLCI; complementary chl-a and turbidity observations; Lake Victoria one of 24 study lakes
verified.where: abstract p.1; table 1 p.3; figs. 9-10 p.12; conclusions p.15

verified.claim: no in-situ validation data for any lake ('large in situ data gaps... prevent direct calibration and validation')

cards.caveat: Not in the app yet: a water-quality layer would need this kind of retrieval plus field checks on Lake Victoria.

cards.question: Where do fires cluster, and in which season?
cards.caveat: No fire study of the basin is in bibliography/ yet - use the layer's year control to look for patterns.

cards.question: How much land burns in a typical year?
cards.caveat: No burned-area study of the basin is in bibliography/ yet - the layer's annual totals are a starting point.

sources.caveats: Tree-cover loss, not deforestation; only where cover 2000 >= 30 %; detection improved ~2011-2013, annual values not strictly comparable across the break. Map shows cumulative loss at 5-year epochs (MapLibre cannot style rasters by value); the panel reports exact annual areas.
sources.citation: Hansen et al. (2013), Science 342:850-853. Data: UMD/Google/USGS/NASA.

sources.title: Active fires (VIIRS)
sources.source: NASA FIRMS VIIRS 375 m active fires; density: S-NPP only (2012-2025); points: S-NPP + NOAA-20 (NOAA-20 archive from 2020); confidence nominal/high
sources.caveats: Mostly savanna and crop-residue burning; charcoal production not detected reliably; cloud hides wet-season fires. NOAA-20 only in the point layer.
sources.citation: NASA FIRMS; Schroeder et al. (2014), RSE 143:85-96. doi:10.5067/FIRMS/VIIRS/VNP14IMGT

sources.title: Burned area (MODIS)
sources.source: MODIS MCD64A1 v6.1 monthly burned area, annual union per ~500 m cell, via Microsoft Planetary Computer
sources.units: burned at least once in the year (0/1)
sources.caveats: ~500 m detection misses small/low-intensity burns; cloud limits wet-season detection.
sources.range_note: annual burned area in the basin, all years 2001-2025: min 4100 km2 (2017), median 10296 km2, max 15323 km2 (2003)

sources.title: Land cover (Esri/IO annual)
sources.source: Esri/Impact Observatory annual LULC v2 (10 m; displayed at 30 m, nearest), via Microsoft Planetary Computer (io-lulc-annual-v02)
sources.period: 2017-2023 (no 2024 release on Planetary Computer at build time, probed 2026-10-21)
sources.caveats: Global land-cover products disagree on cropland in sub-Saharan Africa (Kerner et al. 2023); year-to-year change is indicative.
sources.citation: Karra et al. (2021), IGARSS; Impact Observatory, Esri, Microsoft.

sources.title: Land cover reference (ESA WorldCover 2021)
sources.source: ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200 (displayed at 30 m, nearest)
sources.citation: Zanaga et al. (2022). ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200. doi:10.5281/zenodo.7254221

sources.title: Place names
sources.source: OpenStreetMap via the Protomaps daily basemap (build 2026-10-22, schema v4, Planetiler 0.10.2)
sources.units: labels only: countries, cities, towns, villages (from z11), lakes, rivers, protected areas
sources.citation: © OpenStreetMap contributors (openstreetmap.org/copyright). Basemap tiles: Protomaps (protomaps.com). Fonts: Noto Sans (SIL Open Font License) via protomaps/basemaps-assets.
sources.caveats: Volunteered geographic information: coverage and spelling vary; label positions are OSM points, not authoritative gazetteer locations.

sources.title: Admin boundaries
sources.source: geoBoundaries gbOpen ADM1 + ADM2 (simplified), Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi; clipped to the basin
sources.period: boundary years vary by country (2006-2021; see provenance)
sources.units: ADM1 and ADM2 polygons; names at mid zoom
sources.licence: per boundary - see provenance (Public Domain, CC0, CC BY 4.0, CC BY 3.0 IGO, ODbL); geoBoundaries itself CC BY 4.0
sources.citation: Runfola, D. et al. (2020) geoBoundaries: A global database of political administrative boundaries. PLoS ONE 15(4): e0231866. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0231866
sources.caveats: Boundaries are indicative and not an official delimitation. Uganda ADM1 is the 4 regions (2017, from OSM) and ADM2 the 2006 counties; Tanzania ADM1 is OSM-derived. Not GADM.
